problem: Prior semantic visual navigation (e.g., GCN scene-prior methods with deep RL) has no concrete decision model for multiple objects in one frame, no explicit motion planning, no real-world tests, and needs heavy training.
motivation: Affordable service robots should navigate using only an egocentric RGB camera. Humans find objects by reasoning over visible cues (related objects, zone likelihood, occluders), so a knowledge-based, low-training approach can mimic this.
key_idea: Navigate to a target object using only ego RGB by combining an ontology of object/zone relations (co-location, on-top-of, occlusion) with a GeoSem map that stores per-step landmark scores for backtracking and decision-making.
insight: The paper reports no ablations, so no component is isolated. Its only evidence is a single-scene comparison in which the knowledge-based policy finished faster than 30 humans (about 117 s vs 632 s average), plus one real-robot demo. Semantic priors from Visual Genome co-occurrence, without RL training, can drive plausible search behavior, but the evidence is anecdotal.
method: Knowledge representation: OWL/RDF ontology with SPARQL queries, holding relations locatedAt(object, zone), coLocatedWith, locatedOnTopOf and occlusionBy, learned from Visual Genome frequency statistics
Scene processing: YOLOv3 for fast detection, with a Mask-RCNN fallback when YOLO detects nothing; a Filter module drops frames to match processing speed; the ego view is split into polygonal segments

Decision rule: move toward the segment whose centroid has the maximum sum of relation probability (RP) with the target times detection confidence; prefer doors/openings when zone relation is low; avoid restricted areas and obstacles; go around occluders via free space

GeoSem map: Euclidean grid map from discrete odometry storing per-step direction, detected objects with confidence, and a landmark score (object-target probabilities × zone probability × rotation coverage); enables backtracking on a falling score or dead end
Navigation: 360° scan at start or near openings, Manhattan-style obstacle bypass, and backtracking to the next best landmark point until the target is visible or the search is exhausted

setting.backbone: YOLOv3 detector (with Mask-RCNN fallback) + ontology-based rule decision module
setting.training_data: Pretrained detectors; relation probabilities from Visual Genome frequency statistics; no navigation training
setting.action_space: discrete: forward, backward, rotate left/right (90° or 45°), stop
setting.privileged: none (robot's step size and body dimensions are known; pose from discrete odometry dead-reckoning)

numbers_note: Only a completion-time comparison against 30 human players in one custom Webots scene (Table 1: human min 83 s, max 786 s, avg 632 s; robot avg 117 s). There are no standard benchmark metrics such as SR or SPL. The text says humans took about 6 minutes on average, which conflicts with the table's 632 s.
results: In one custom Webots room with target 'orange', the robot finished in about 117 s on average versus 632 s for 30 human players (table). A real-world office demo on a Double2 robot found a 'cup' by reasoning over 'bottle', 'table' and 'chair'.
limitations: Evaluation is anecdotal: one simulated scene, one target, one real demo, with no standard benchmarks, success rates, or baselines
Dynamic obstacles are out of scope, and dead-reckoning drift is not handled; depth is not used
Relies on discrete actions and hand-crafted thresholds and parameters (α, β), with a text/table mismatch in reported human times
builds_on: Spatial semantic visual navigation with GCN scene priors (Kiran et al.)
